https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgj.text: Image source, SAPS Image caption, South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates By Basillioh Rukanga Published 23 September 2026, 07:23 BST Updated 3 hours ago At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban. Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said. Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched". While the motive of the shooting has not yet confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings". "Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died. A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car. The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects. South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day. In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country. Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg. Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities. In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police. https://www.courant.com/2026/09/19/its-a.text: UConn students pass the William Benton Museum of Art on UConn’s main campus in Storrs on Tuesday, March 24, 2026. (Aaron Flaum/Hartford Courant) By Kimberly Phillips | UConn Today PUBLISHED: September 19, 2026 at 5:35 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... No birthday is complete without gifts (and cake), and this fall the William Benton Museum of Art marks its 60th with both – an exhibition-sized thank you to the friends who’ve given gifts over the last decade and a celebration that closes an online silent auction (and also includes cake). “This museum is part of UConn’s history,” curator and academic liaison Amanda Douberley says. “We help UConn tell its story, in part through all these amazing gifts from faculty, alumni, and friends of the museum. They’re like a wish for the future, to say, ‘I’m giving this to you, so it can be part of this institution’s story.’” The Benton’s own story starts in 1933, when former UConn President Charles Lewis Beach bequeathed his art collection to the University and left a trust fund to allow for the continued acquisition of more. A hundred years ago, Douberley says, it was even more difficult than today to get to big museums in Boston and New York; back then because travel was slow, and today because life is fast. Places like the Benton, which formally opened in 1966 as simply the Museum of Art before taking the name of the U.S. senator in 1972, offer people a similar experience, only closer to home. "Between Known and Unknown" by Vibha Galhotra sits on display in the "With Gratitude: Highlights from a Decade of Gifts" exhibition in the William Benton Museum of Art on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Sydney Herdle/UConn Photo) It’s a place now where people can see work from French neo-impressionist Maximilien Luce, whose “Portrait of the Sculptor Albert Marque” is on display; art professor Ray DiCapua, whose recently donated work “Marie” also is on display; and various pieces of African art, also on display, thanks to donations from sociology Professor Emeritus Josef Gugler and his wife Janine Gugler. They’re all part of the museum’s latest exhibition, “With Gratitude: Highlights from a Decade of Gifts .” With more than 7,500 objects in its full collection, the museum is featuring a fraction of the more recent acquisitions but aims to show visitors the breadth of its holdings. “We have very limited funds to make purchases, so we rely on gifts, like a lot of museums do, to build our collection,” says Douberley, who curated the show. “We have 17th century altarpiece sculptures from Austria, 18th century illustrated manuscript leaves from India, and 19th century American portraits from Coventry, Connecticut. Across time, across space, and across media, there are so many different kinds of things that come into the collection.” Collecting Stories … Those altarpieces from Austria come from Board of Trustees Distinguished Professor of History Emeritus Richard D. Brown and his wife, retired human development and family sciences associate professor Irene Quenzler Brown. The two were in France in the mid-1960s as Fulbright Scholars when they discovered the two statues of St. Dominic and St. Catherine of Siena from the early 1600s in an antique store in Germany during Christmas break. But they didn’t buy them at first. “We learned their price and returned to France. But they stayed in our minds and several weeks later we decided to take the plunge,” Richard Brown writes in a “Collecting Story” wall label next to the sculptures by Erasmus Kern . In 2019, Douberley says, the Browns donated them to the museum. “We oftentimes don’t have these stories behind the objects in our files,” she says. “We’re not an archive, where you would keep everything together from a single donor in one collection. Here in the museum, we categorize objects by the artist’s nationality, size, and medium, so collections get taken apart. “One thing we did for this show to highlight our donors and the really interesting stories about the objects was to invite a handful of donors to share the story behind the art,” she continues. “For these two altarpieces, knowing a little more about the life these objects had with these faculty members, from their early career all the way through, is very special.” … and Sharing Stories Three circa-1830s paintings from artist Erastus Salisbury Field are enjoying their first time on display at the Benton after having just been restored following their acquisition from donor Pamela Dewey in 2022. Benton Director Nancy Stula says the three, depicting Anna and Roderick Dimock and their daughter Sophia Ann Dimock, were stored in a private residence in Coventry and were in rough condition, one with a tear in it, when a local antiques dealer working on behalf of the family brokered their donation. “They’re very typical of limner works, itinerant artists who went from place to place,” Stula says of the portraits. “This particular artist stopped in Coventry and painted six portraits of this family – the father, mother, and daughter, as well as a servant and two sons.” "Marie" by Ray DiCapua reflects off the glass of the frame containing "La Robe de Chambre Rouge [The Red Dressing Gown]" by Henri Manguin in the "With Gratitude: Highlights from a Decade of Gifts" exhibition in the William Benton Museum of Art on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Sydney Herdle/UConn Photo) The “Collecting Story” label says Field came to town and sought a room at the Brigham Tavern, where George Washington once stopped for a meal in 1789, albeit some 40 years earlier. To pay for his room and board, Field made the paintings, paying off his debt to Anna Brigham Dimock, who owned and operated the tavern, and Roderick Dimock, who ran the farm. Dewey, a descendant of the family, owned the three portraits of Anna, Roderick, and Sophia, while another relative owned then later sold the portraits of the sons. The portrait of the servant girl once was on display at the Nathan Hale Homestead, the story label goes on to say. Another “Collecting Story” label shares details of an exchange program started by printmaking Professor Emeritus Gus Mazzocca with the Academy of Fine Arts in Krakow, Poland. The program brought 12 artists from Poland to UConn and sent eight UConn faculty members to Poland. The program also included UConn students who studied in Krakow. Douberley says she chose “A Dream About Rock Beach and Big Fish” by Stanislaw Wejman and “Bajka” by Anna Sobol-Wejman for the latest exhibition, etchings that depict a fairytale and a dreamscape and provide a look at Polish art when it was a communist country. Silent Auction and Celebration In the neighboring gallery at the museum, where the exhibition “Colors in the Dark: Ellen Carey” shows off the artwork of the abstract photographer who creates her pieces in pitch black darkrooms, Stula says Carey has been particularly generous to the Benton in her donation of a large photo to the museum’s online silent auction. She’s offered her 2026 piece “Dings & Shadows.” “We have gift certificates to a number of restaurants from Max Downtown to Tree House Brewing, Michael Jordan’s Steakhouse, and Dog Lane Café,” Stula says. “We have paintings and works of art from some of our donors, like Douglas Hyland from the New Britain Museum of American Art. We have items from artists who are on faculty, like Janet Pritchard and Kathryn Myers. We have 70 items total, and there’s something for everyone.” Pieces of artwork sit on display in the "With Gratitude: Highlights from a Decade of Gifts" exhibition in the William Benton Museum of Art on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026. (Sydney Herdle/UConn Photo) But there are two items that have Benton staff particularly abuzz: a pair of one-of-a-kind paintings by Jonathan XV, who smeared primary colors onto paper with his nose and tongue, then signed each with his pawprint. “Those are going to be a real hit because people just love Jonathan,” Stula says. Other items include: a private violin concert with UConn strings professor and acclaimed musician Solomiya Ivakhiv, a full set of hardcover “I Spy” books signed by author Walter Wick, tickets to the Hartford Stage production of “Dracula,” tickets to The Boston Pops Holiday Concert at Jorgensen Center for the Performing Arts, hand-carved wooden bowls by artist and Benton preparator Kerry Smith, along with many other items. The online auction is now open and closes at 4 p.m. on Sunday, Sept. 27, with a birthday party at the museum (that, of course, includes cake). Details on how to register for the auction are available on the museum’s website. “Proceeds from the auction help us to expand the possibilities for education and to fulfill our mission,” Douberley says. “Many of our donors give generously just so students can interact with art. People often ask us after a show where it all goes, because they think it’s in here all the time. It goes into storage, but you can always see it in our database online. Even when it’s not on display, it’s still part of our story.” “With Gratitude: Highlights from a Decade of Gifts” and “Colors in the Dark: Ellen Carey” are open until Dec. 20. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Iracema Ferreira and her Portuguese dictionary, which she brings with her to class. ‘It’s for some occasional questions about words that some insist are in Brazilian,’ she said. Photograph: Gabriel Ferreira Morais View image in fullscreen Iracema Ferreira and her Portuguese dictionary, which she brings with her to class. ‘It’s for some occasional questions about words that some insist are in Brazilian,’ she said. Photograph: Gabriel Ferreira Morais Portugal ‘It’s glottophobia’: Brazilians in Portugal battle for linguistic recognition Brazilian speech therapists say struggle for acceptance is part of wider prejudice embedded into Portuguese society Gabriel Ferreira Morais in Lisbon Sun 4 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google N ot long after she started studying to become a nurse in Portugal , Iracema Ferreira began bringing a dictionary to her classes as a retort to accusations she was speaking Brazilian, not Portuguese. “It was to show that those words are in the Portuguese language dictionary,” she said. A Brazilian speech therapist, Ferreira moved to Portugal in 2020 and later heard from several colleagues from her home country that the process of getting a licence to work in the European country was a dead end. The 45-year-old soon abandoned the idea of continuing the career she had practised for a decade and switched to nursing instead. The speech therapists’ struggle for recognition underlines what Brazilians say is a wider strand of prejudice still embedded into Portuguese society against the language variant of its former colony. “It’s glottophobia,” said Tanise Anhaia, president of the Brazilian Speech Therapists Association in Portugal (AFBP), using a term to mean linguistic discrimination. View image in fullscreen Tanise Anhaia now presides over the Brazilian Association of Speech Therapists in Portugal, which aims to have more political power and advocate for a more transparent process. Photograph: Gabriel Ferreira Morais Barely any Brazilians have been awarded a licence to practise as a speech therapist in Portugal since 2019, according to the AFBP, which was set up last year. One of the two exceptions is a woman whose lawyer argued his client’s rejection was “totally incomprehensible, illegal and unconstitutional” and got it overturned. For many Brazilians in Portugal the struggle will not come as a surprise. People from the Latin American giant make up by far the largest migrant group, numbering more than 480,000, according to the Portuguese migration agency, AIMA. (According to the Brazilian foreign ministry, the population is larger, at 628,000 in 2025.) However, as the size of the group increases, so do the reports of xenophobia. In 2022, the commission for equality and against racial discrimination reported that “Brazilian nationality” was the most common basis of discrimination in the complaints they received, forming 34% of all complaints. View image in fullscreen Iracema Ferreira says she heard from a professor that paciente (patient) was used only in Brazil. However, she’s heard it used by Portuguese people and the word is included in her Portuguese dictionary. Photograph: Gabriel Ferreira Morais In 2023 Statistics Portugal reported that 55% of Brazilians said that they had suffered discrimination, the biggest proportion in terms of nationality. Last year a Portuguese man was arrested after posting a video in which he offered 500 euros for each “Brazilian head” delivered to him. A Brazilian woman who lives in the Lisbon district, who asked to remain anonymous, told the Guardian she had seen her then eight-year-old being punched by another child and told: “That’s for Brazilians to learn that they have to go back to their land.” Earlier, at a school meeting, she remembered a teacher saying “the kids were speaking too ‘Brazilianised’” and that they would themselves receive speech therapy. The popularity of Brazilian YouTubers is leading to more young people emulating the speech of their favourite stars, say parents and linguists. In the 1980s there was a similar panic in Portugal over the popularity of Brazilian soap operas, said Afrânio Barbosa, dean of the Centre for Letters and Arts at Brazil’s federal university of Rio de Janeiro. “Every time a Brazilian cultural product spreads in Portugal there is such a reaction. And you hear the same sentences: ‘They are worsening the Portuguese language’,” said Barbosa. “These are social reactions due to a colonial symbolic projection of the language, as if its legitimacy lay in its geographical origin and not in the historical demographic identity of its speakers.” Brazil and Portugal are part of the Community of Portuguese Speaking Countries, which has the “diffusion of the Portuguese language” as one of its goals. Yet the question of whether the variants in practice are different languages or not splits linguists. “It’s a very complex discussion,” said Renato Basso, a professor of linguistics at the federal university of São Carlos who studies the history of the Portuguese language. “The Brazilian Portuguese spoken by people with a university degree from the urban centres and the European standard are relatively similar.” In schools it’s important that everyone has access to a “standard norm”, added Basso. However, linguists point out that even within Brazil and Portugal, people end up speaking differently depending on where they live and their social circle. “If you get stuck with the idea that there is only one version of a language, everything gets too complicated,” said Basso. That seems to be exactly what speech therapists are being told, however. When Anhaia sat the test to get a licence in 2021, there was no linguist present, just a speech therapist, she recalled. At the end, the examiner told her: “I won’t approve you because you don’t speak European Portuguese.” Anhaia will sit the test again this year. Margarita Correia, a Portuguese linguist, said the requirement was “absurd”. The body responsible for the licences, ACSS, said that some candidates lacked the knowledge to assess the Portuguese population and that their university degrees were not equivalent. The ACSS declined to comment. The Portuguese Association of Speech Therapists said its members did not have the authority to comment. Álvaro Filho, a Brazilian journalist and writer who has lived in Lisbon since 2016, assembled chronicles of life as a migrant for his new book Eu Não Falo Brasileiro (I Don’t Speak Brazilian). One of them is about his son, whose teacher said that “he would just pass the class if he spoke Portuguese”. “It’s implicit that when they say you speak Brazilian it’s because they don’t recognise this Portuguese variant as an equal. It’s worse,” he said. “It might become an autonomous version, but it has to be our decision, from Brazil.” Explore more on these topics Portugal Brazil Linguistics Americas Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.straight.com/movies/vancouve.text: Today » 13°C Wed 19°C Thurs 17°C Fri 20°C Movies Movie Reviews Movies Features Television 1 of 2 2 of 2 Get the best of Vancouver in your inbox, every Tuesday and Thursday. Sign up for our free newsletter . Vancouver, B.C., and St. John’s, Newfoundland and Labrador, are both Canadian coastal cities. The obvious comparisons kind of stop there. At least that’s what actor Mackenzie Davis, who grew up in West Vancouver, found when she went to the easternmost province to film the new Netflix suspense thriller Below . “It felt otherworldly,” she says on a video call with the Straight . “It’s so far away. I kept like zooming in and out on the map and going across and seeing Vancouver, and just it's so far from where we grew up.” Davis did find some similarities eventually. “The people are really warm and really excited to have you there and so proud of their home province, which I think is a quality of British Columbians as well. Every day you’re like, ‘This is a beautiful place to live,’ and that just doesn’t go away. The people there couldn’t wait to show us stuff and include us and share their homes with us; it was so nice.” Below is the brainchild of Toronto showrunner Jesse McKeown (producer/writer of The Umbrella Academy ), who fell in love with Newfoundland on a trip there 18 years ago. The original idea that McKeown pitched Netflix—basically Jaws but in Newfoundland, he says in a press release—has been fleshed out more fully. In the show, Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett) is a widowed fisherman who has taken to selling chunks of ice to vodka brands. When an unidentified sea creature starts wrecking havoc on the town, Calvin teams up with marine biologist Fonda Howander (Davis) to investigate. Davis, who is known for films and shows like Halt and Catch Fire , Station Eleven , Blade Runner 2049 , and Happiest Season, is fairly selective of the roles she plays. Though she’s been in hot demand, this is only her fifth major role since 2021. “It felt like a show I would watch. I thought it was really smart, and I loved Jesse's voice—it was obviously steeped in his experience of Newfoundland,” says Davis, who spends most of her time in London these days, on why she decided to take the literal plunge. “It’s my dream to do things that hold many things at once. I want something to be thought-provoking but funny. And silly but also serious. And moving but light. And this had all of it.” While the show features some suspensions of reality, it’s also grounded in its setting. Below takes place during Come Home Year, a real tradition when former residents return home to the province. The town that Calvin and Fonda live in, Snook’s Arm, is going through a resettlement vote—an official process where residents of remote outposts decide whether to accept government compensation packages to abandon their communities and shut down public services. The real Snook’s Arm was relocated in 2017. Davis, along with Hartnett and co-star Charlie Heaton of Stranger Things, who plays one of Calvin’s sons, had their hands full learning the Newfoundland accent. Davis, who says she had never heard it before living on the West Coast, found it challenging to pinpoint. But the specificness of the show was part of the appeal. “It doesn’t feel like it could be anywhere. This is about a place and a people, and that matters. The mark of a good writer is that they’re telling stories that are universal in their specificity.” That universal specificness applies to her character, too. Davis didn’t hit the textbooks to study up on marine biology. “Early on in my career, I really wanted to do every ounce of homework and really just know everything about a thing as proof that I deserved to be there,” she says. “But I don’t think immersing myself in the career of a marine biologist is that important because it’s more about the emotional resonance of discovery and existential fear and knowledge that people aren’t taking seriously. There are lots of things there that I have access to that don’t require a degree.” She also didn’t work too hard to develop a chemistry with Hartnett, but it’s definitely there. We’ve only seen the first two episodes of the show, but a romance is lightly hinted at between the two. “You kind of either like someone or you don't, and then you can fake it, and you’re like, ‘I’m the best actress in the world; everyone thinks I like this person, and I do not like them,’” she says with a laugh. “But Josh is a delight. He's so kind and cool and very low-key and smart. And he's curious and just like a lovely person to be around. So there wasn't a lot of work required.” Growing up in Vancouver, Davis never had any doubts that she wanted to be an actor. “I was just one of those kids that liked doing it—I did lots of plays at school and camps and stuff like that. And then I watched tons of movies as a kid too,” she says, noting that some of the foundational films of her childhood were titles like Death Becomes Her , Beetlejuice , Princess Bridge , and Drop Dead Fred . Davis’s parents, entrepreneurs John and Lotte Davis , now live on the Sunshine Coast, and Davis visits her home province a couple of times a year. Asked for some establishments and places that she misses, she shouts out Zen Japanese Restaurant in West Vancouver, Granville Island, and Nook in Kitsilano. Next on the docket for her are a couple of ambitious projects. “I have a film that I shot at the same time as Below last year by a Hungarian director who I love very much,” she says about Lili Horvát’s My Notes on Mars , which is currently playing festivals around the world. She also has another Netflix production due out in the coming months called The Undertow , in which she plays opposite Jamie Dornan. “I'm kind of just focusing on those right now, and, you know, waiting for a good script,” she says.
